correctness.rationale: At most two selected cells occur per row or column because the collinear geodesic is unique. Manhattan diameter ≤3 bounds the span in each coordinate. For a row span of three, the extremes are singletons on the same column, so equality at six forces two cells in each intermediate row; the extremes forbid columns farther than one away, and their vertical geodesic forbids their own column on the intermediate rows. For smaller row span, six requires three consecutive rows of two cells; width two is too small and width three would leave one omitted cell per row and column. Such omissions cannot hit both opposite-corner pairs, since any two corners chosen from distinct opposite pairs share a row or column. The only remaining span is three in the column coordinate, giving the transposed equality argument. The listed six geodesic representatives for H cover all pairs under the two reversals and certify feasibility, and no orientation/translation is counted twice. On 3×3, a center-containing five-set would need two adjacent corners and two edge midpoints. With top corners, these midpoints must be bottom and left or right; in either case all monotone paths from the corresponding top corner to the bottom midpoint hit the center or the chosen side midpoint. Without the center, one corner and four midpoints is blocked by the midpoint on the corner-to-opposite-side-midpoint path; two adjacent corners prohibit the intervening midpoint and thus force all other midpoints. The feasible sets are the four rotations of B. Independent BFS subset enumeration found exactly the expected optimizer families on 3×3, 3×4, 4×3 and 4×4.
residual_risks: The independent finite grids do not prove the theorem on larger grids; the span proof does. The frozen script visits all nonempty bounded-diameter cliques but skips visibility testing once a candidate is smaller than the current best. This does not affect the computed optimizer families. The frozen 13-grid output was not independently rerun.
